newsitem.title: UK: Dlr eases in late Europe, mulls German asset row.
newsitem.headline: Dlr eases in late Europe, mulls German asset row.

text.p: The dollar was easier above its afternoon lows in late European trade against the mark and yen, finding little clear direction in the growing tension between the Bundesbank and German government over plans to revalue German assets.
Earlier today, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel indicated the government's desire to pursue the scheme, saying such a revaluation was necessary despite the Bundesbank's objections.
"It's still an uncertain position," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy. "Waigel has reasserted his position and he is unwilling to give ground to the Bundesbank."
Dealers said the revaluation row, seen as a bid by the German government to bolster its finances to help it meet monetary union criteria, has confused markets.

Dollar/mark rose overnight following the German central bank's strong objections on Wednesday to the government's plans, on grounds that the scheme would only have short-term benefit and would undermine the credibility of EMU.

"The implication is still unclear about Germany, nothing has really been cleared up," said a UK bank dealer. "It's wait-and-see for now and it will be like that at least until we get the French election out of the way."
The second round of French parliamentary elections are on Sunday. Mark/French franc has retreated from Wednesday's four-month highs, seen amid growing expectations of a Socialist win.

By 1510 GMT, the dollar stood at 1.6969/74 marks against a session high of 1.7067 but up from late Wednesday's 1.6902/07 marks in Europe. Dollar/yen stood at 115.99/6.09 from earlier highs of 116.55 and late Wednesday's 115.45/50.

Analysts said if the German government succeeds in pushing through its revaluation plans, it raises the prospect of a timely, broad-based EMU with a potentially diluted euro which is seen dollar positive and mark negative.
On the other hand, the Bundesbank can make life difficult for the government by being unhelpful over Germany's EMU preparations and raise the risk of a delay to the project.
"Both scenarios are equally likely to happen, the implication is one of volatility," said CIBC's Coleman.
Elsewhere, the Swiss franc gained slightly against the mark and dollar after the Swiss National Bank's decision to leave its discount rate unchanged.
Dealers had not expected a Swiss cut today, but the central bank's addition of liquidity in the money market recently to dampen franc strength prompted some speculation of a cut.
Dollar/Swiss franc was trading at 1.4123/33, down from a session high of 1.4226 and late Wednesday's 1.4150/60.
There was little reaction to U.S. weekly jobless claims data earlier, unchanged at 322,000 from the previous week and in line with expectations.
U.S. data Friday includes revised U.S. first quarter GDP and first quarter implicit deflator. Chicago May PMI data and the final May Michigan business sentiment survey is also due tomorrow.
